Based on the kits used by the Iowa State University College of Education, particularly through their "Checkout STEM" outreach program, you are likely looking for littleBits.

These kits are a staple in ISU’s educational outreach because the components (or "Bits") are color-coded and snap together using magnets. This magnetic connection ensures that the pieces can only be connected the "right" way, making them ideal for young learners to explore circuitry without the risk of short-circuiting or needing complex wiring.

Here are the primary magnetic electronic kits used in educational environments like Iowa State:

Modular Magnetic Electronics

These sets are designed for open-ended play, allowing children to snap together power sources, sensors, and outputs (like lights or motors) to create functional gadgets.

  • The Little Bits Educator Starter Kit is the most common version seen in classrooms. It includes a variety of Bits that teach fundamental concepts like engineering, physics, and design thinking through a screenless, hands-on experience.
  • For home use or smaller projects, the Little Bits Cloudbit Starter Kit provides 6 essential modules to build interactive projects and learn the basics of how electronics communicate.

Advanced Magnetic Building

If the kit involved more technical or stackable components, it might have been a system like Microduino, which is often used for higher-level STEM projects.

  • The Microduino Mcookie Magnetic301 Expert Kit features stackable, magnetic modules that are compatible with LEGO. This allows kids to build complex electronic systems directly into their brick creations.
  • The Microduino Advanced 202 Kit is designed for beginners who want to transition into coding and programming. It uses magnetic modules to eliminate messy wiring while teaching Arduino-based logic.

Snap-Together Logic Blocks

While not always purely magnetic, these blocks are frequently used in Iowa school districts for teaching logical thinking and circuit flow.

  • The 4M Logiblocs Smart Circuits Kit uses plug-and-play blocks to build gadgets like intruder alarms or metal detectors. They are color-coded by function, helping kids understand the logic behind an electronic circuit.
